claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase FCC/B2 lamellar microstructure.
The untreated starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and a brittle failure mode.
Dislocation pile-ups near lamellar phase boundaries cause local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining.
Low-temperature annealing can precipitate ordered L12 particles within the FCC phase of a lamellar FCC/B2 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The annealing-induced L12 precipitates are coherent and nanoscale.
The L12 precipitates will also be dispersed along internal phase boundaries.
Fine L12 precipitates impede dislocation motion through obstacle strengthening, including Orowan bowing and bypass.
Impeding dislocation motion with L12 precipitates will reduce dislocation accumulation and pile-ups at internal phase boundaries.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups will diminish local stress concentrations at internal boundaries.
The precipitate-containing microstructure will promote more uniform plastic deformation through back-stress hardening.
The proposed treatment will delay the initiation or propagation of microcracks.
The treatment will increase room-temperature elongation to failure relative to the untreated material.
The treatment will maintain or increase yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated material.
Achieving the benefit requires a precipitate size and spatial distribution that avoid coarsening.
Excessive annealing or inappropriate annealing temperatures may coarsen the precipitates and negate the mechanical-property benefit.
Room-temperature tensile testing at a quasi-static strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1 is applicable to this alloy and treatment.
The proposed benefit is primarily applicable to eutectic high-entropy alloys having similar dual-phase lamellar microstructures.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome allows strength merely to be maintained, whereas the falsification rule can be read as falsifying the hypothesis if strength shows no improvement. Thus, an outcome of improved ductility with unchanged strength is permitted by the prediction but may be rejected by the stated rule.
